## TL;DR

Expanded the Android Hub fixture QA sweep to exercise portrait and landscape
phone dimensions and every supported theme/appearance combination. The final
headless Playwright run passed 302 of 302 checks. It found no reproducible
layout defect, so no styling change was needed. The expanded test script and
session evidence are recorded in `mobile/scripts/fixture-qa.ts` and
`docs/qa/2026-11-android-hub-third-pass.md`.

## Work and rationale

I read task #1192 and the preceding Hub fixture QA report for task #1171. That
report already contained useful checks for long server names, long URLs and
unbroken server-provided text, but it tested only 360px and 412px portrait
viewports. The third pass was specifically about rotation and themes, so I
extended the retained browser QA script instead of creating a second harness.
The viewport matrix now uses 360 × 800 and 412 × 915 portrait sizes, with
800 × 360 and 915 × 412 rotated sizes. All four sizes run the seven picker and
form fixtures, lock settings and lock retry checks.

For theme switching, the script opens Settings, selects each of the eight
design themes, and selects System, Light and Dark appearance in turn. It checks
the document's theme and resolved appearance attributes, its CSS color scheme,
that the page background is not transparent, and that the Settings screen
remains in bounds. System mode is evaluated using the headless browser's
current color-scheme preference. This verifies the mode wiring and rendered
theme token application in that environment; it does not claim to represent
every Android device's system setting.

I extended the long-name case to all four viewport dimensions. In addition to
checking the overall viewport bounds, the script confirms the server row fits
its list/card region and its overflow-menu button remains visible. The long URL
edit sheet and add-form error cases also run at all four dimensions. The
unbroken URL and remote-text wrapping cases remain in the sweep. Existing
fixture checks still cover empty, connected, unavailable and discovery views,
and lock enable/failure/retry behavior.

The QA result is documented separately in the new dated QA record. I recorded
the browser, dimensions, assertions and results, plus the boundaries of what
the run can establish. The test is a headless Chromium viewport simulation. It
does not prove behavior on a real Android handset or Android WebView, and its
fixture discovery data does not test live servers or tailnet calls.

## Approaches tried

I first attempted to run the existing fixture sweep immediately after starting
Vite. That server had resolved Vite from the root package before the mobile
dependencies were installed, so it could not resolve Capacitor imports and
the app never mounted. The lock-settings locator then timed out. I installed
the mobile package from its existing `bun.lock` using `bun install
--frozen-lockfile`, stopped that initial Vite process, and restarted the
requested `bunx vite --port 5188` in `mobile/`. The page then mounted cleanly
and the original 55-check sweep passed.

The first expanded matrix attempt exposed a test selector issue: the visible
appearance buttons use title case, while the new script initially requested
lowercase names with an exact, case-sensitive role match. This was a harness
failure rather than an app bug. I changed the locator to use a case-insensitive
exact regular expression and reran the complete script. The corrected matrix
passed. That run showed 295 checks before I noticed that the new long-name
bounds assertion still covered only its first viewport. I adjusted the script
to loop that case over all four sizes and ran it again. The final count was 302
checks, all passing.

## Challenges and blockers

No product bug or unresolved blocker was found. The main operational issue was
dependency resolution from the already-running Vite process; restarting after
the frozen mobile install fixed it. The other failures were in the new QA
script's accessible-name selector, corrected before the final run. No
screenshots were retained, and no device-level evidence is claimed. A human
device QA pass would still be needed to establish actual Android WebView,
system bar, cutout and keyboard behavior.

## Key learnings

The earlier picker and text-wrap regression coverage was reusable and already
passed at the narrower and wider portrait widths. Rotation coverage needed
explicit wide, short viewports rather than merely naming a phone width, so the
matrix pairs each portrait width with its rotated dimensions. Theme checks are
more informative when they validate resolved document state and geometry after
each control action, rather than only confirming that each select option
exists. Finally, long-name coverage must exercise each viewport directly;
passing the ordinary fixture across a matrix does not demonstrate how
truncated user data behaves. The reusable script now keeps those distinctions
explicit for future Hub QA.
